'''Harold ("Hal") Warren Lewis''' (born October 1, 1923<ref name="Oral">[http://www.aip.org/history/ohilist/4742.html Oral History Transcript--Harold Lewis] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101013010859/http://www.aip.org/history/ohilist/4742.html |date=2010-10-13 }} at the Center for History of Physics, [[American Institute of Physics]]</ref> – May 26, 2011<ref name="ucsb">{{cite journal|author=|title=Campus Notes|date=June 2011|volume=21|issue=8|url=http://www.ia.ucsb.edu/93106_archived/2011/June/notes.html|access-date=9 June 2011|archive-date=24 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924032129/http://www.ia.ucsb.edu/93106_archived/2011/June/notes.html|url-status=dead|journal=93106, News for the Faculty and Staff of the University of California Santa Barbara|via=}}</ref>) was an American [[Emeritus]] Professor of [[Physics]] and former department chairman at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] (UCSB).  He was chairman of the [[JASON Defense Advisory Group]] from 1966 to 1973, and was active in US government investigations into safety of nuclear reactors.

In his 1990 book ''Technological Risk'' he warned of the risks of global warming. In 2010, after 67 years of membership, he resigned from the [[American Physical Society]], citing what he saw as  "the global warming scam, with the (literally) trillions of dollars driving it”.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/201011/memberresigns.cfm|title = APS Responds to Member's Resignation over Climate Change}}</ref>

==Career as a physicist==
Lewis entered [[New York University]] in 1940 and graduated in physics. He earned a master's degree from the [[University of California, Berkeley]], from 1943 to 1944 before joining the Navy, where he served in [[World War II]] as an electronics technician.<ref name="Oral"/> After the war, he returned to the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and earned his Ph.D. in Physics studying under [[J. Robert Oppenheimer]]. His focus was [[Particle physics|high-energy physics]] ([[Cosmic ray|cosmic rays]] and [[Elementary particle|elementary particles]]). He, along with the other theoretical physics professors at Berkeley, refused to sign the [[McCarthyism|McCarthy era]] [[loyalty oath]] on principle, and in 1950 went to Princeton. Later, when offered reinstatement at Berkeley, he chose instead to accept a position at [[Bell Labs]], where he did research on superconducting materials. In 1956, he left [[Bell Labs]] to join the [[University of Wisconsin, Madison]] to work on solid-state physics and plasmas. In 1964, he left to join the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] as a full professor, and later chairman, in their growing physics department. He retired from UCSB in 1991.<ref name=ucsb/>

He wrote a text on the trade-offs between technological advances and risks,<ref name="tech risk">H. W. Lewis, ''Technological Risk'', W.W.Norton, 1992 {{ISBN|0-393-30829-4}}</ref> and also authored a popular book on decision-making.<ref>H. W. Lewis, ''Why Flip a Coin: The Art and Science of Good Decisions'', Wiley, 1997 {{ISBN|0-471-16597-2}}</ref> In 1991, Harold Lewis won. the [[Science Writing Award]] for his book 'Technological Risk'.<ref name="tech risk"/><ref>[http://www.aip.org/aip/writing/winsci.html AIP Science Writing Award winners] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101014020254/http://aip.org/aip/writing/winsci.html |date=2010-10-14 }}</ref>

Lewis was chairman of the [[JASON Defense Advisory Group]] from 1966 to 1973, when he worked on the issue of missile defense.<ref name="Oral"/> He was a long-term member of the [[Defense Science Board]] (DSB),<ref name="Oral"/> and chaired a 1985 DSB Task Force (with [[Stephen Schneider (scientist)|Stephen Schneider]]) on [[nuclear winter]].<ref>Lawrence Badash, 2009,  ''A nuclear winter's tale: science and politics in the 1980s'', [https://books.google.com/books?id=y8M5vx-Lrk0C&pg=PA163 p. 163]. MIT Press, {{ISBN|0-262-01272-3}}</ref>   Lewis was active in the field of safety of [[nuclear power plant]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |pmc=1911929 |last1=Lewis |first1=HW | title= Nuclear power plant malfunctions: potential types of exposure and severity |journal=Bulletin of the New York Academy of Medicine |volume=59 |issue=10 |pages=898–903 |year=1983 | pmid = 6582976 }}</ref>  In 1975, he chaired a year-long study of [[light-water reactor]] safety for the [[American Physical Society]] (APS).<ref>{{cite journal | title= Nuclear reactor safety—the APS submits its report |journal= [[Physics Today]] |date=July 1975 |volume= 28 |issue= 7 |page= 38 |doi=10.1063/1.3069053 |bibcode= 1975PhT....28g..38. |last1= Lewis |first1= Harold W. }}</ref>
Lewis chaired the 1977-1979 [[Risk Assessment]] Review for the US [[Nuclear Regulatory Commission]].

==Views on climate change==
In his 1990 book ''Technological Risk'', Lewis wrote that "all models agree that the net effect" of increasing [[greenhouse gas]]es "will be a general and global warming of the earth; they only disagree about how much. None suggest that it will be a minor effect, to be ignored while we go about our business." Reducing the effects, including significant sea level rise, would "require global cooperation and sacrifice now, to avert something far in the future, and a conjectural something at that. There is no evidence in human history that is in the cards, but one can always hope."<ref name="Revkin" />

In a letter dated 6 October 2010, Lewis wrote to [[Curtis Callan]], President of the [[American Physical Society]] (APS), resigning from the society. Lewis said that he had joined the APS 67 years previously, when it was "as yet uncorrupted by the money flood" which he said had "become the [[Wiktionary: raison d'être|raison d’être]] of much physics research, the vital sustenance of much more, and it provides the support for untold numbers of professional jobs." In his view, it was "the global warming scam, with the (literally) trillions of dollars driving it, that has corrupted so many scientists, and has carried APS before it like a rogue wave. It is the greatest and most successful pseudoscientific fraud I have seen in my long life as a physicist." This letter of resignation was made public, and "Lewis was vaulted to celebrity status by conservative and [[contrarian]] Web sites and commentators".<ref name="Revkin">{{cite news|last=Revkin| first= Andrew| url = http://dotearth.blogs.nytimes.com/2010/10/15/a-physicists-climate-complaints/ | title= A Physicist's Climate Complaints| work=New York Times| quote=One week ago Lewis was vaulted to celebrity status by conservative and contrarian Web sites and commentators when he disseminated his letter of resignation ...| date=October 15, 2010}}</ref> On 12 October, the [[climate change denialist]] [[think-tank]] The [[Global Warming Policy Foundation]] announced that Lewis had agreed to join their "Academic Advisory Council".
 
On 12 October, 2010, the APS issued a statement that there was no truth in Lewis's accusations; it pointed out that the vast majority of its membership works in areas not dealing with climate change, and its policy statements were developed in accordance with strict ethical standards.<ref>{{cite web | title=APS Comments on Harold Lewis' Resignation of his Society Membership | website=APS Physics | date=12 October 2010 | url=https://www.aps.org/newsroom/pressreleases/haroldlewis.cfm | access-date=20 May 2016}}</ref> The APS completely rejected Lewis's claims of "scam" and "fraud", stating that virtually all reputable scientists were agreed on observations of human caused [[global warming]]. In a personal reply, Callan criticized Lewis's disrespectful allegations about colleagues. Responding to complaints Lewis raised alleging rejection of a petition for a Topical Group on Climate Science, Callan said the proposal had been accepted and was being implemented, but unfortunately Lewis had decided to resign rather than participate.<ref>{{cite web | publisher = APS | title=APS Responds to Member's Resignation over Climate Change | url=https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/201011/memberresigns.cfm }}</ref>

==Personal==
His father was a textile salesman who immigrated from Russia{{When|date=September 2011}}; his mother was born in the United States. He had two older brothers. He met his future wife Mary at UC Berkeley. They had two children, and later moved to Santa Barbara, California, in 1964.
